items.prompt: Founder invests ₹50 lakh. Construct Journal Entry, Ledger, Trial Balance, Opening Balance Sheet.
items.answer:
Journal Entry: Debit Cash ₹50,00,000; Credit Share Capital ₹50,00,000 (entry je_0001, balanced: True).
Ledger: Cash account debited ₹50,00,000; Share Capital account credited ₹50,00,000.
Trial Balance: Cash ₹50,00,000 (debit) = Share Capital ₹50,00,000 (credit) — balances: True.
Opening Balance Sheet: Assets ₹5,000,000 = Liabilities ₹0 + Equity ₹5,000,000. No liabilities exist because the founder contributed capital, not debt — the accounting equation is established at the moment the company is born.

items.prompt: Company purchases machinery for ₹20 lakh cash. Show impact today and five years later.
items.answer:
TODAY: Journal Debit Machinery ₹20,00,000; Credit Cash ₹20,00,000 — Buy a fixed asset for cash: Machinery ↑ ₹2,000,000 (Balance Sheet) Cash ↓ ₹2,000,000 (Cash Flow Statement (Investing)) No Income Statement effect today. Over time: The asset is depreciated over its useful life in future periods. → Depreciation Expense increases each period → EBIT decreases. → Lower EBIT → lower PBT → lower PAT in those future periods. Balance Sheet: one asset (Cash) exchanges for another (Machinery); total assets unchanged. Cash Flow: a ₹20,00,000 Investing outflow.
FIVE YEARS LATER (straight-line over a 5-year life, ₹4,00,000/year): Accumulated Depreciation reaches ₹2,000,000 (the full original cost), Net PPE falls to ₹0 — the asset is fully depreciated. Cash does NOT change again from depreciation (-2,000,000 → -2,000,000) — the cash outflow already happened today, in Investing activities; each year's Depreciation Expense reduces EBIT and PAT with zero further cash effect.

items.prompt: Company sells ₹12 lakh goods on credit; customer pays after 90 days. Trace both dates.
items.answer:
AT SALE (Day 0): Journal Debit Accounts Receivable ₹12,00,000; Credit Revenue ₹12,00,000. Income Statement: Revenue recognised at ₹1,200,000 — Revenue is recognised on delivery via Accounts Receivable, NOT cash. Cash does not increase; the sale still counts toward this period's Income Statement. Balance Sheet: Accounts Receivable = ₹1,200,000. Cash Flow: no effect (Cash = ₹0).
AT COLLECTION (Day 90): Journal Debit Cash ₹12,00,000; Credit Accounts Receivable ₹12,00,000. Income Statement: UNCHANGED (Revenue still ₹1,200,000 — Cash increases and Accounts Receivable decreases — revenue is NOT recognised again; it was already earned when the sale occurred.) Balance Sheet: Accounts Receivable falls to ₹0. Cash Flow: an Operating inflow of ₹12,00,000 (Cash rises to ₹1,200,000).

items.prompt: Company receives ₹5 lakh advance, no goods delivered. Explain Revenue/Cash/Liability.
items.answer:
Revenue: ₹0 — no revenue is recognised because nothing has been delivered yet; recognising revenue on cash receipt alone would violate the revenue recognition principle.
Cash: increases by ₹5,00,000 — the cash was genuinely received today.
Liability: Unearned Revenue increases by ₹500,000 — this represents the company's obligation to deliver goods/services in the future; it converts to Revenue only when that obligation is fulfilled. Cash increases but revenue is NOT recognised — a liability (Unearned Revenue) increases instead, because the obligation to deliver has not been satisfied.

items.prompt: Salary expense accrued but unpaid. Explain.
items.answer: Journal: Debit Salary Expense ₹1,50,000; Credit Salary Payable ₹1,50,000. Under accrual accounting, the expense is recognised the moment the obligation arises (work performed), NOT when cash is eventually paid. Income Statement: PAT falls by the full ₹1,50,000 (PAT = ₹-150,000). Balance Sheet: Salary Payable (a liability) rises to ₹150,000. Cash Flow: no effect today (Cash = ₹0) — Salary Expense increases and Salary Payable (liability) increases — cash is unchanged; the obligation exists the moment the work is done, not when paid.

items.prompt: PAT increases. Cash decreases. Explain every possible reason.
items.answer: PAT increasing while Cash decreases can have several independent causes, and more than one can be true at once: Depreciation: Depreciation reduces PAT (via EBIT) but is a non-cash expense — it is added back when computing Operating Cash Flow. | Revenue recognised without cash collected: A credit sale increases PAT via Revenue, but if Accounts Receivable increases, cash has not yet been collected — the increase in Receivables is subtracted in the Cash Flow Statement. | Inventory build-up: Buying inventory ahead of sales increases the Inventory asset without any Income Statement effect yet, consuming cash that PAT does not reflect. | Expenses accrued but not yet paid: Salary/Interest/Tax due but unpaid reduce PAT immediately, but conserve cash until actually paid — increasing the related payable adds cash back in the Cash Flow Statement relative to PAT. | Cash received before revenue is earned: Deferred/Unearned Revenue increases cash with no PAT effect — the opposite direction of the credit-sale case above. In one line: PAT is an accounting measure of value created; Operating Cash Flow is a measure of cash actually moved — depreciation, working capital, and accrual timing are exactly what separates the two.

items.prompt: Inventory doubles. Revenue is flat. Interpret.
items.answer: Inventory doubling while Revenue stays flat: Inventory grew +100.0% while Revenue grew only +0.2% — may indicate demand slowdown (unsold stock building) or a deliberate strategic build ahead of expected demand. Total Assets grew +14.3% while Revenue grew only +0.2% — the asset base is growing faster than revenue — capital intensity is rising, which should show up in ROCE/ROIC. Working Capital grew +90.9% while Revenue grew only +0.2% — growth is consuming disproportionately more working capital — exactly why PAT can rise while cash flow falls. Total Assets grew +14.3% while Revenue grew only +0.2% — the balance sheet is growing faster than the top line — capital intensity is rising.

items.prompt: Receivables increase 60%. Revenue increases 10%. Interpret.
items.answer: Receivables +60% against Revenue +10%: EBITDA grew +45.5% while Revenue grew only +10.0% — suggests strong operating leverage — cost discipline is amplifying revenue gains into profit. Receivables grew +60.0% while Revenue grew only +10.0% — signals collection risk or aggressive revenue recognition — receivables are outpacing the sales that created them. Gross Profit grew +25.0% while Revenue grew only +10.0% — implies gross margin expansion — improved pricing power or cost control per unit sold. Working Capital grew +66.7% while Revenue grew only +10.0% — growth is consuming disproportionately more working capital — exactly why PAT can rise while cash flow falls.

items.prompt: Debt increases. Interest expense falls. Possible? Explain.
items.answer: Yes, this is possible — Debt and Interest Expense are not mechanically tied in the same direction within a single period. Plausible explanations: (1) the new debt was raised late in the period, so the average balance used to compute interest expense is still low; (2) the company refinanced older, higher-rate debt with new, lower-rate debt — the balance rose but the effective rate fell enough to reduce total interest; (3) a shift in the debt mix toward instruments with lower coupons (e.g. government-linked or subsidised borrowing). Cash declining WHILE debt is rising is a classic financial-stress signal — the business is burning liquidity and replacing it with borrowed capital rather than internally generated cash.

items.prompt: Depreciation doubles. Cash unchanged. Explain why.
items.answer: Depreciation doubling has NO effect on Cash because it is a non-cash allocation of an asset's cost that was already paid for in cash when the asset was purchased. The non-cash allocation of a fixed asset's cost over its useful life. Believing depreciation reduces cash — it reduces PAT but is added back in the Cash Flow Statement. Doubling it only reduces EBIT and PAT further (via a higher non-cash charge) and would, if anything, INCREASE the gap between PAT and Operating Cash Flow, since a larger non-cash add-back is required to reconcile the two.

items.prompt: Revenue +20%, PAT +25%, OCF -30%. Interpret.
items.answer: Revenue +20%, PAT +25%, OCF -30% — PAT growing faster than Revenue while Operating Cash Flow falls is a textbook earnings-quality warning: profit growth is not cash-backed. Earnings Quality score: 4.0/10 (Low quality — cash conversion and/or accrual signals are weak). EBITDA grew +41.7% while Revenue grew only +20.0% — suggests strong operating leverage — cost discipline is amplifying revenue gains into profit. Gross Profit grew +28.9% while Revenue grew only +20.0% — implies gross margin expansion — improved pricing power or cost control per unit sold.

items.prompt: EBITDA +18%, FCF -40%, Capex doubled. Interpret.
items.answer: EBITDA growing while Free Cash Flow falls sharply and Capex roughly doubles is a reinvestment-phase pattern, not necessarily a red flag on its own: FCF is what actually funds dividends, buybacks, and debt paydown without external financing — a company can report growing PAT for years while FCF stays negative if capex or working capital consumes it all. EBITDA grew +18.5% while Revenue grew only +10.0% — suggests strong operating leverage — cost discipline is amplifying revenue gains into profit. Gross Profit grew +13.3% while Revenue grew only +10.0% — implies gross margin expansion — improved pricing power or cost control per unit sold.

items.prompt: Working Capital absorbs ₹500 crore. What does that mean?
items.answer: Working Capital absorbing ₹500 crore means that amount of cash is trapped funding the operating cycle (receivables + inventory, net of payables) rather than being available as free cash flow — even a highly profitable, growing business will show Operating Cash Flow roughly ₹500 crore lower than PAT plus non-cash add-backs would otherwise suggest. A growing business often needs MORE working capital even while highly profitable — this is precisely why PAT can rise while Operating Cash Flow falls. This is exactly why growth can be genuinely profitable on the Income Statement while consuming, not generating, cash.

items.prompt: Inventory↓ Receivables↓ Cash↑ Revenue flat. Interpret.
items.answer: Inventory and Receivables both falling while Cash rises, with Revenue flat, is a working-capital RELEASE — the business is collecting faster and de-stocking, freeing up cash without needing revenue growth to do it. This is a genuine cash-generation positive, but flat Revenue alongside an inventory drawdown is also consistent with management pre-emptively cutting stock ahead of an anticipated demand slowdown — the direction of forward orders/guidance would disambiguate the two. Receivables fell -38.5% and Inventory fell -40.0% in the same period — whether this is favourable depends on what Inventory represents: a decline is a positive signal if Inventory is a cost/expense/working-capital item (inventory is growing faster than receivables — the working-capital drag is shifting toward the stocking side), and a negative signal if it represents value creation.

items.prompt: PAT falls. ROE rises. Explain.
items.answer: PAT fell (₹160 → ₹130) while ROE rose (0.2667 → 0.2889) — this happens when the Equity base shrinks faster than PAT falls, typically from buybacks or dividends exceeding retained profit. ROE is a RATIO: if the denominator (Equity) shrinks by a larger proportion than the numerator (PAT), the ratio rises even on lower profit — decompose via DuPont before crediting this to operating improvement. Operating Expenses increased +6.7% while Gross Profit declined -5.0% — operating expenses are growing faster than gross profit, compressing EBITDA margin. ROE increased +8.3% while PAT declined -18.8% — ROE is improving even as PAT itself is not growing as fast — decompose this via DuPont: it likely reflects a shrinking equity base (buybacks/dividends) rather than pure operating improvement.

items.prompt: Current Ratio falls. Quick Ratio rises. Explain.
items.answer: Yes — Current Ratio moved 2.6667 → 1.875 (fell) while Quick Ratio moved 1.3333 → 1.375 (rose). This happens when Inventory (excluded from the Quick Ratio) falls sharply while Cash and Receivables (both still counted in the Quick Ratio) hold steady or improve — the mechanical exclusion of a shrinking, low-liquidity asset from Quick Ratio's numerator lets it diverge from Current Ratio.

items.prompt: ROCE rises. ROE falls. Possible? Why?
items.answer: Yes — ROCE moved 0.3559 → 0.4407 while ROE moved 0.2667 → 0.2333. ROCE (EBIT / Capital Employed) measures operating returns independent of financing; ROE (PAT / Equity) is leverage-sensitive. Paying down debt and raising fresh equity improves the underlying operating business (ROCE up) while simultaneously diluting the leverage-boost to shareholder returns (ROE down) — the two ratios can legitimately diverge whenever the capital structure itself changes materially.

items.prompt: Debt/Equity rises. Interest Coverage rises. Interpret.
items.answer: Yes — Debt/Equity moved 0.4 → 0.7 (up) while Interest Coverage moved 4.0 → 7.5556 (also up). This is possible when new debt funds a high-return investment that grows EBIT faster than the incremental interest expense it creates — leverage is rising, but the earnings base servicing it is rising even faster, so the business is arguably using the debt productively rather than riskily, at least by this metric alone.

items.prompt: Gross Margin falls. EBITDA Margin rises. Possible?
items.answer: Yes — Gross Margin moved 0.45 → 0.4 (fell) while EBITDA Margin moved 0.17 → 0.22 (rose). This happens when operating-expense discipline (SG&A cuts, restructuring, headcount reduction) more than offsets input-cost pressure or pricing weakness at the gross-profit level — the two margins measure different parts of the cost structure and can move in opposite directions. Gross Profit fell -11.1% and Operating Expenses fell -35.7% in the same period — whether this is favourable depends on what Operating Expenses represents: a decline is a positive signal if Operating Expenses is a cost/expense/working-capital item (operating expenses are growing faster than gross profit, compressing EBITDA margin), and a negative signal if it represents value creation.

items.prompt: Asset Turnover falls. ROIC rises. Explain.
items.answer: Yes — Asset Turnover moved 1.25 → 1.1111 (fell, since the asset base grew with flat Revenue) while ROIC moved 0.1222 → 0.3286 (rose). This is a DuPont-style offset: margin expansion (lower COGS/OpEx as a share of Revenue) improved after-tax operating profit enough to outweigh the drag from a larger, less-efficiently-utilised capital base — turnover and margin are two separate levers that can move in opposite directions while still improving the combined return metric.

items.prompt: Goodwill triples. Revenue unchanged. Interpret.
items.answer: Goodwill tripling while Revenue is unchanged means an acquisition has been made (or a revaluation occurred), but its economic benefit has not yet shown up in the top line — either because integration takes time, the acquired entity's revenue isn't yet consolidated at scale, or the price paid did not reflect near-term revenue synergies. This concentrates future impairment risk: if the acquired business never delivers the expected revenue/earnings, the Goodwill balance will eventually be written down, hitting PAT in a single period. Red flags detected: 3.

items.prompt: Revenue grows; Receivables/Inventory grow faster; Cash falls. Interpret.
items.answer: This is a compounding working-capital drag: Revenue growing more slowly than both Receivables and Inventory, with Cash falling, means the business is funding its own growth by trapping more cash in the operating cycle than the growth itself generates — a pattern consistent with either aggressive channel-stuffing (pushing goods/credit to book revenue) or genuinely under-managed working capital during a growth phase. EBITDA grew +45.5% while Revenue grew only +10.0% — suggests strong operating leverage — cost discipline is amplifying revenue gains into profit. Receivables grew +80.0% while Revenue grew only +10.0% — signals collection risk or aggressive revenue recognition — receivables are outpacing the sales that created them. Inventory grew +70.0% while Revenue grew only +10.0% — may indicate demand slowdown (unsold stock building) or a deliberate strategic build ahead of expected demand. Red flags detected: 4 (high severity: 1).

items.prompt: Company repeatedly adjusts EBITDA. Explain the risk.
items.answer: Repeatedly adjusting EBITDA (excluding 'one-off' items every single period) is itself a red flag: if an item recurs period after period, it is not actually one-off — it is a real, recurring cost of doing business that management is choosing to exclude from the headline metric. One-off cost cuts (furloughs, deferred maintenance) can flatter EBITDA margin temporarily without reflecting a sustainable structural improvement. The risk is that investors anchor on an 'adjusted' EBITDA that consistently overstates sustainable operating profitability, masking a genuine deterioration in the underlying, unadjusted business.

items.prompt: OCF negative, Net Income positive, 3 consecutive years. Interpret.
items.answer: Operating Cash Flow negative for three consecutive years while Net Income stays positive is a severe, structural earnings-quality red flag — it means the accounting profit is being generated entirely through non-cash items or working-capital timing (or both) for a sustained period, not a one-off. This pattern historically precedes covenant breaches, emergency financing, or restatement in a meaningful share of cases; it should be treated as a near-disqualifying signal until fully explained. Red flags detected across the series: 5 (high severity: 4).

items.prompt: Dividend payout exceeds Free Cash Flow. Interpret.
items.answer: Dividends of ₹90 against Free Cash Flow of ₹70 means the payout is NOT fully covered by cash the business generates — the shortfall must be funded from existing cash reserves or new borrowing. Dividends funded from FCF are sustainable; dividends funded by drawing down cash or raising debt are not — a coverage ratio below 1x for multiple periods is a warning sign. Dividends Paid increased +50.0% while Free Cash Flow declined -36.4% — the dividend is growing faster than the free cash flow that funds it — a sustainability risk if the gap persists. Red flags detected: 2.

items.prompt: Institutional Reasoning — analyst note for a multi-signal scenario.
items.answer: ANALYST NOTE. Revenue grew 12%, but Gross Margin compressed while EBITDA Margin expanded — this combination suggests input-cost or pricing pressure at the gross-profit level that was more than offset by operating-expense discipline (SG&A/overhead control) below the gross-profit line. Capex roughly doubling with Total Debt unchanged indicates the expansion is being self-funded from internal cash rather than new borrowing — consistent with the Operating Cash Flow decline observed, which likely reflects a combination of the capex-funding working-capital build (Receivables and Inventory both rose materially) and the reinvestment itself. PAT rising even as OCF falls is a genuine earnings-quality watch item: the profit is real on an accrual basis, but is not yet being converted into cash at the same rate — worth monitoring over the next 1-2 periods to confirm this is a temporary reinvestment/working-capital effect rather than a structural cash-conversion problem. Supporting evidence: EBITDA grew +58.8% while Revenue grew only +12.0% — suggests strong operating leverage — cost discipline is amplifying revenue gains into profit. Receivables grew +50.0% while Revenue grew only +12.0% — signals collection risk or aggressive revenue recognition — receivables are outpacing the sales that created them. Inventory grew +44.4% while Revenue grew only +12.0% — may indicate demand slowdown (unsold stock building) or a deliberate strategic build ahead of expected demand. Revenue grew +12.0% while Gross Profit grew only +4.4% — implies gross margin compression — costs are eating into the incremental revenue.

items.prompt: Impossible Questions — honesty about insufficient evidence.
items.answer:
Q: PAT doubled. What happened?
A: There isn't enough information to determine the cause of the pat change. Several explanations are possible (margin expansion (higher gross or EBITDA margin), a lower effective tax rate, lower interest expense (debt repayment or refinancing), a one-time or non-operating gain, etc.), and additional evidence (such as interest_trend, margin_trend, one_off_items_flag) is required to distinguish between them.
Q: Revenue grew. What happened?
A: There isn't enough information to determine the cause of the revenue change. Several explanations are possible (volume growth, pricing or realisation increase, a favourable product/customer mix shift, an acquisition consolidating new revenue, etc.), and additional evidence (such as acquisition_flag, mix_data, pricing_data) is required to distinguish between them.
Q: ROE improved this quarter. Why?
A: There isn't enough information to determine the cause of the roe change. Several explanations are possible (improved net margin, improved asset turnover, a change in financial leverage, a shrinking equity base from buybacks or dividends, etc.), and additional evidence (such as asset_turnover_trend, equity_base_trend, leverage_trend) is required to distinguish between them.
Q: EBITDA increased. Explain why.
A: There isn't enough information to determine the cause of the ebitda change. Several explanations are possible (revenue growth, gross margin expansion, operating expense reduction / cost discipline, a change in accounting classification between COGS and OpEx, etc.), and additional evidence (such as gross_margin_trend, one_off_items_flag, opex_trend) is required to distinguish between them.
Q: The cash balance went up. Why?
A: There isn't enough information to determine the cause of the cash change. Several explanations are possible (operating cash generation, a financing event (new debt or equity raised), an investing event (asset sale or reduced capex), working capital release (collections, inventory reduction), etc.), and additional evidence (such as financing_cf_trend, investing_cf_trend, operating_cf_trend) is required to distinguish between them.
